title: Bow a clean two-second open A on a full-size violin held up in the other hand
instruction: Pick up the violin and play its open A string with the bow: one clean, steady note of at least two seconds. Then lay the bow and the violin back in their places on the cloth.
context: Bowing a violin is recognised in a second: school orchestras, street players and concert halls all start from one long, even bow on an open string, a beginner's first lesson. The tone is a precise physical act. A bowed string speaks cleanly only while the hair stays on that one string, moves steadily across it near the bridge and presses inside a force window that narrows toward the bridge (Schelleng's diagram; measured on a violin by Schoonderwaldt, Guettler and Askenfelt, Acta Acustica 2008): too hard and it crunches, too light or too slow and it whistles or dies, and a bow tilted one string's angle too far sounds two strings. A violin isn't played lying down: one hand holds it up while the other draws the bow.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A dark green wool felt cloth, 5 mm thick, from 12 to 90 cm forward and from 47 cm right to 34 cm left, fixed. (2) A full-size (4/4) student violin, 0.45 kg, balance point 10.5 cm into the body from the neck: spruce top and maple back and ribs under orange-brown varnish, body 356 mm long (bouts 168, 112 and 208 mm wide, pointed corners, f-holes, purfling), ribs 30 mm, plates arched 14-15 mm; maple neck and scroll with four ebony pegs; ebony fingerboard 270 mm long, 24 to 42 mm wide, running out 140 mm over the body; maple bridge 195 mm from the body's top end, its top on a 42 mm arc with the strings 11 mm apart; nut to bridge 327 mm; four strings G3 D4 A4 E5 (the A aluminium-wound on a synthetic core); ebony tailpiece with an E fine tuner, ebony chinrest, end button; 59 cm long in all. A black clip-on tuner is clipped to the scroll. The violin lies on its back on the cloth across the robot's view: scroll to the left, the E string on the far side, the middle of its body 40 cm forward and 12.6 cm right, its neck joining the body 5.2 cm left of the centre line. (3) Its bow, 75 cm long and 60 g, balancing 20.5 cm in front of the frog's middle: a round pernambuco-brown stick tapering from 8.4 to 5.8 mm with a slight camber, an ebony frog 46 x 14 x 26 mm with a pearl eye and silver ferrule, a head with an ivory-white face, and a white horsehair ribbon 10 mm wide and 66 cm long, tensioned and rosined. It lies hair down on the cloth, pointing forward, frog toward the robot: the frog's middle 16 cm forward and 40 cm right. Both arms start at their home pose. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot. Real trial: the violin and bow of a Stentor 1400 Student I 4/4 outfit (US$268.99), the A string tuned to A4 (440 Hz); a Snark SN-5 or D'Addario NS Micro clip-on tuner (US$15-17) on the scroll; a felt cloth with tape marks round the violin's outline and at the bow's frog and head; a strip of masking tape on the violin's top beside the A string, marked 11 mm and 55 mm from the bridge; a camera with a microphone facing the tuner. Rosin dust stays on the hair and strings; the grippers touch only the frog and the fingerboard's edges.
scoring: Latched for the rest of the trial (score 0.0): the violin or the bow falls (drops faster than 0.5 m/s), or a gripper's fingertips go into the violin's body. The A string sounds at a step when all of these hold: the violin is held up (its lowest point 2 cm or more above the cloth); the bow's hair touches the A string and no other (a string within 0.4 mm of the hair counts as touched); the contact is 1/30 to 1/6 of the string length from the bridge (11 to 55 mm); the bow moves along its length across the string at 5 cm/s or more, square to it within 15 degrees; and the hair presses on the string with a force F between 0.69 mN / beta^2 and 0.91 N s/m x speed / beta, beta being the contact's distance from the bridge over the string length (the bow-force limits measured on a violin's open string, Schoonderwaldt, Guettler and Askenfelt 2008: 91 mN / beta at 10 cm/s, rising with speed). A clean open A: the A string sounds for 2 s with no break longer than 0.1 s (a bow change fits in that) and no other string touched in that span. 1.0: a clean open A of 2 s at some point, and at the end the violin lying back in its place (its origin at the neck joint within 3 cm of its start, turned less than 10 degrees, flat on the cloth within 10 degrees, not held), the bow lying back in its place (the frog's middle within 4 cm of its start, turned less than 10 degrees, on the cloth, not held), and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm); 0.75: the 2 s note played, the end state not met; 0.5: a clean open A of 0.5 s or more at some point; 0.25: at some point the hair touched the strings while the violin was held up; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit or once the full score has held 1 s with the violin and the bow still. Real trial: the tuner on the scroll shows A (440 Hz) with its needle steady in the green, and the microphone records one steady tone; the 2 s and any break are timed on the video. A crushed tone (too much force), a whistling or dying one (too little force, too slow) or two strings sounding shows as no steady A on the tuner and is heard on the audio. The video shows the hair on the A string alone, between the tape marks 11 and 55 mm from the bridge, the bow moving, and the violin clear of the cloth. Falls, a gripper striking the body, the end positions against the tape marks and the arms against their start marks are judged from the video and the end photo.
reset_notes: Lay the violin on its back on the cloth inside its tape outline, scroll to the left, tuner on the scroll; lay the bow hair down inside its tape marks, frog toward the robot. Check the A string is in tune (tuner shows A).
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim, PhysX, 20 Hz), real sizes and masses. Strings are rigid 1.2 mm bars; the hair is a rigid ribbon on a sprung slide on the stick (300 N/m, 8 mm travel, design values). The tone is computed each step from contact, bow-bridge distance, speed, squareness and force against the published bow-force limits for a violin's open D string (none are published for the A); no sound is simulated. The violin collides as boxes and cylinders. Cameras 1280x704.
